beginner: The US economy is growing steadily at 2.8% this year, which means businesses are hiring and people have jobs.
Inflation is cooling - we expect it down to 2.2% by the end of 2026, so your groceries and gas should stop getting more expensive so fast.
The Federal Reserve is expected to keep interest rates steady around 3.25%, which affects how much it costs to borrow money for a car or house.
moderate: Real GDP growth is tracking at 2.8% for 2026, slightly above the full-year forecast of 2.2%, signaling the economy remains resilient despite higher borrowing costs.

Core PCE inflation is expected to fall to 2.2% by year-end, suggesting the Fed's rate hikes are working, though the current account deficit sits at 3.8% of GDP reflecting America's reliance on foreign capital.
With unemployment holding near 4.2%, the labor market remains tight enough to support consumer spending even as the budget deficit widens to 7.5% of GDP, a structural headwind for long-term growth.
expert: Real GDP growth at 2.8% is outpacing the 2.2% full-year forecast, driven by resilient consumer spending and business investment; core PCE inflation declining to 2.2% creates room for the Fed to hold rates at 3.25% through 2026 rather than cutting aggressively.

The unemployment rate anchored near 4.2% masks persistent labor market bifurcation, with wage growth in services offsetting weakness in goods-producing sectors, while the 7.5% budget deficit and 3.8% current account deficit signal reliance on foreign financing to sustain growth.

Forward guidance hinges on whether core inflation can sustain its 2.2% trajectory without a demand shock, since nominal wage growth remains elevated at 4%+ year-over-year, creating vulnerability if external shocks force central bank policy tightening in 2027.

beginner: Canada's economy is slowly getting better in 2026 after struggling in 2025, though growth will still be quite weak.
The Bank of Canada is expected to cut interest rates to 2.25%, which should help businesses and homeowners save money on loans.
Inflation in Canada is expected to stay calm at around 2%, so prices should remain stable for Canadian shoppers.
moderate: Canadian GDP growth is expected to firm modestly in 2026 following subdued performance in 2025, but at 1.7% growth, the economy remains significantly weaker than the US and UK, reflecting persistent household debt challenges and weak business investment.

The Bank of Canada's policy rate falling to 2.25% reflects confidence that inflation will remain anchored at 2%, though the unemployment rate climbing to 6.5% signals the central bank is prioritizing growth support over inflation concerns.

Canada's current account deficit sits at only 0.5% of GDP, the smallest among major economies, but this strength masks underlying domestic demand weakness that rate cuts alone cannot solve without fiscal stimulus or rising business confidence.
expert: GDP growth tracking at 1.7% represents a meaningful acceleration from 2025's performance, yet remains structurally constrained by household debt at 97% of disposable income and a business investment cycle that has not recovered from the 2020 shock.

The Bank of Canada's anticipated rate cut to 2.25% signals a dovish pivot despite inflation holding at 2%, suggesting officials view slack as the primary risk; this diverges from the Fed's stance and should weaken the Canadian dollar through 2026 if the differential persists.

Forward growth depends critically on whether lower rates translate into mortgage refinancing demand or accelerate household deleveraging, with the unemployment rate likely to breach 6.5% before stabilizing, creating political pressure for larger fiscal transfers that would delay deficit reduction below the 1.5% GDP forecast.

beginner: The UK unemployment rate will keep climbing until March 2026, then level off, meaning fewer people will be finding jobs soon but things will stabilize.
Inflation in Britain is expected to drop to 2.2% by spring 2026, so price increases should finally slow down for ordinary families.
The Bank of England is expected to cut interest rates to 3%, making it cheaper to borrow money and potentially helping the housing market recover.
moderate: UK unemployment is expected to rise until March 2026 before stabilizing at around 5%, a pattern that contrasts sharply with the tight US labor market and reflects structural weakness in business investment and consumer confidence.
Headline inflation is forecast to decelerate to 2.2% in Q2 2026, giving the Bank of England room to cut its policy rate to 3% and support a sluggish 1.5% GDP growth rate that lags peers.

The current account deficit remains elevated at 2.5% of GDP despite the energy crisis of 2022-2023 fading, indicating underlying competitiveness challenges that interest rate cuts cannot address and that may require sterling depreciation to correct.
expert: Unemployment rising until March 2026 and then stabilizing at 5% represents a lagging adjustment to weak demand in 2024-2025, with the Bank of England's anticipated rate path falling to 3% priced in by markets, though forward guidance hinges on whether wage growth sustains inflation at target.

Headline inflation deceleration to 2.2% in Q2 2026 is driven by energy base effects and subdued wage growth rather than demand destruction, creating a policy environment where the Bank of England can cut aggressively without triggering market repricing of terminal rates.

The 2.5% current account deficit alongside 1.5% GDP growth and a 4.2% budget deficit creates a fiscal-external account imbalance that suggests sterling could face depreciation pressure in 2027 if gilt yields rise globally, forcing the Bank to balance domestic growth support against currency stability.

beginner: Japan's economy is slowing at 0.8% growth in 2026, which means the country is not creating much wealth or new jobs.
Inflation in Japan is expected to stay very low at 1.8%, so the Bank of Japan will likely keep interest rates near 1.25% to encourage borrowing and spending.
Japan has a strong current account surplus of 4.8% of GDP, meaning the country saves more than it spends and is lending money to other nations.
moderate: Japan's GDP growth of 0.8% in 2026 reflects persistent demographic headwinds and low productivity growth, a structural challenge that contrasts sharply with the 2.8% rate in the US and suggests Japan's growth trajectory will remain constrained despite accommodative policy.

Inflation remaining at 1.8% gives the Bank of Japan the flexibility to hold its policy rate near 1.25%, the lowest among major economies, though this ultra-loose stance reflects decades of deflation scarring and the central bank's reluctance to normalize even as employment tightens to 2.5% unemployment.

Japan's 4.8% current account surplus is the only positive reading among major economies, powered by a structural trade surplus and foreign investment income, yet this strength masks domestic demand weakness that low rates and fiscal transfers cannot overcome without productivity gains.
expert: GDP growth at 0.8% represents a deterioration from 2025 performance, driven by aging population headwinds, weak business investment, and deflationary expectations that keep real interest rates high despite the Bank of Japan's 1.25% nominal rate, creating a policy trap.

The 1.8% inflation forecast sits significantly below the Bank of Japan's 2% target, signaling that demand remains chronically weak; the central bank's reluctance to exit accommodative policy despite 2.5% unemployment reflects institutional fear of demand destruction if rates normalize too rapidly.

Japan's 4.8% current account surplus will likely persist through 2026, but forward growth depends on whether productivity reforms can offset demographic decline, since fiscal stimulus will prove unsustainable if GDP growth does not accelerate above 1.5% and the central bank cannot credibly commit to rate normalization by 2028.

beginner: Germany is getting help from its government spending more money, which should push the economy forward slightly this year.
Trade tensions are easing up, which means German companies might sell more stuff abroad without worrying as much about tariffs.
The jobless rate should stay low at 3.8%, so most people who want to work can find a job.
moderate: Euro area growth forecast came in at 1.3% for 2026, driven by German fiscal expansion that contrasts sharply with the austerity of previous years. Reduced tariff threats from global trade negotiations are lifting business confidence after months of uncertainty.
Germany's current account surplus of 4.5% of GDP reflects its export-dependent economy, but domestic consumption will need to strengthen for growth to accelerate beyond the modest 1.3% forecast.
With unemployment at 3.8% and inflation near the ECB's 2% target, Germany has room to sustain higher government spending without overheating the labor market.
expert: The 1.3% euro area growth forecast reflects German fiscal multiplier effects from expanded spending, which should offset persistent weakness in southern Europe and France's structural stagnation. Current account surplus of 4.5% of GDP signals ongoing external imbalance within the currency union despite cyclical improvement.

German fiscal expansion operates in an environment where the ECB holds rates at 2.50% and core inflation remains anchored near 2%, creating space for demand-side stimulus without triggering monetary tightening. The tariff de-escalation removes downside risk to manufacturing output in 2026.

Forward momentum hinges on whether fiscal impulse translates to durable consumption growth rather than precautionary saving, given demographic headwinds and pension reform uncertainty that could constrain multiplier effects below historical precedent.

beginner: France's economy is expected to grow at the same slow pace it did last year, around 1.3%, which means not much is changing.
Consumer spending is holding up, so French people are still buying things and keeping the economy from getting worse.
Unemployment is higher here than in Germany at 7.7%, so finding a job is tougher for French workers.
moderate: Euro area growth forecast of 1.3% represents stagnation for France relative to its 1.4% full-year forecast, with structural labor market issues keeping unemployment at 7.7% despite resilient consumer spending. France lags Germany's fiscal firepower and Italy's recent reforms that are driving modest comparative outperformance.

Consumer spending resilience in France reflects purchasing power preserved by wage indexation and lower energy costs, but productivity growth remains subdued and the budget deficit at 4.8% of GDP constrains further stimulus room.
The current account deficit of 1% of GDP signals ongoing competitiveness challenges in tradable sectors, limiting France's ability to export its way out of low-growth equilibrium.
expert: France's 1.4% full-year growth forecast masks quarterly volatility driven by consumption volatility and volatile fiscal transfers, with the economy tracking near consensus despite structural headwinds in manufacturing and services tradables. The 4.8% budget deficit reflects both cyclical weakness and structural spending commitments that constrain fiscal space.

Labor market rigidity keeps unemployment at 7.7%, the highest in the euro area excluding non-core economies, even as consumer confidence holds firm. ECB rates at 2.50% provide limited relief for debt-servicing costs given France's elevated sovereign spreads relative to Germany.

Downside risk to 2026 growth concentrates on consumer confidence fragmentation across income deciles and potential fiscal retrenchment pressure if bond markets reassess France's deficit trajectory, particularly if euro area growth disappoints below 1.2%.

beginner: Italy's economy will grow around 1.3% this year, helped by the government spending money and people continuing to buy things.
The jobless rate of 5.6% is reasonable and inflation is stable, so households have some security in their wallets.
Italy is earning more money from selling stuff abroad than it spends on imports, which strengthens its position in Europe.
moderate: Euro area growth forecast of 1.3% represents upside surprise for Italy relative to its 1% full-year GDP forecast, driven by fiscal stimulus and consumer spending resilience that outpace structural expectations. Italy's unemployment at 5.6% is lower than France but still higher than Germany, reflecting regional labor market segmentation.

Fiscal stimulus effectiveness in Italy depends on whether spending reaches productive investment or crowds into consumption and transfers, a pattern that has constrained multiplier effects historically. The current account surplus of 0.8% of GDP reflects tourism recovery and manufacturing strength in the north.
Italy's 3.2% budget deficit sits between Germany's restraint and France's excess, positioning Rome for modest confidence from bond markets while maintaining room for demand support.
expert: Italy's growth forecast of 1.3% for the euro area (versus 1% domestic forecast) implies fiscal multiplier effects from stimulus packages are exceeding baseline expectations, particularly in tourism and domestic services where demand reacted sharply to spending announcements. Consumer spending remains resilient despite inflation squeeze from energy costs in late 2025.

The 5.6% unemployment rate masks significant regional divergence between the industrialized north and structurally weaker south, where fiscal transfers have concentrated but productivity gains remain elusive. Current account surplus of 0.8% of GDP reflects manufacturing competitiveness gains but narrows relative to 2024 due to import recovery.

Forward acceleration depends on whether fiscal stimulus locks in through capital formation or dissipates into transfer-dependent consumption, a distinction crucial for evaluating whether Italy's growth can sustain above 1.5% beyond 2026 without structural labor market reforms.

beginner: China's economy is expected to grow 4.8% this year, which is slower than the 5% most people think of as normal for China.
China is selling a lot more stuff to other countries than it buys from them, which means money is flowing in from abroad.
The government is controlling prices well with inflation at around 2%, so savers and workers aren't getting squeezed.
moderate: China's real GDP growth projection of 4.8% for 2026 reflects structural deceleration from the property crisis and aging demographics, despite recent stimulus measures. Current account surplus expected to rise to 4.1% of GDP from 3.5% in 2025 signals export strength offsetting weak domestic demand.

The 4.8% growth forecast sits below China's 5% policy target, signaling that monetary and fiscal stimulus have not yet reignited investment-led expansion. Unemployment at 5.1% remains officially stable, though underemployment in youth cohorts exceeds reported figures.

China's external surplus widening to 4.1% of GDP despite domestic weakness reflects global trade shifts rather than competitive strength, as Chinese manufacturers absorb orders relocating from other Asian suppliers.
expert: Real GDP growth projection of 4.8% reflects the output gap between structural potential (4.2% to 4.5%) and current momentum, where fiscal stimulus and credit easing are extending growth without reversing the property contraction's drag. Current account surplus rising to 4.1% of GDP versus 3.5% in 2025 signals demand destruction at home coupled with export market share gains from geopolitical trade redirection.

The policy rate at 2.75% provides 75 basis points of cut capacity relative to the prior cycle low, but further easing carries diminishing returns if debt-to-GDP ratios exceed 280% across the public and quasi-public sectors. Inflation anchored at 2% masks significant sectoral deflation in tradables and property services.

2026 growth trajectory depends critically on whether credit impulse from new stimulus packages (estimated 5% to 6% of GDP) sustains through year-end or front-loads into Q1, with downside risk if property stabilization remains elusive and youth unemployment accelerates beyond official 5.1% readings.

beginner: India's economy is growing faster than almost any other major country right now, which means more jobs and higher paychecks for workers.
Tech companies in India are selling more products around the world, bringing money into the country and boosting growth.
When an economy grows this fast, prices can rise quickly, so the central bank will watch inflation carefully to make sure it does not get out of control.
moderate: India's 6.7% growth rate in 2026 outpaces most peer emerging markets and reflects strong exports in high-value tech sectors combined with real wage gains that are fueling domestic consumption.
This momentum contrasts sharply with Latin America's 2.3% expansion and Africa's subdued outlook, positioning India as a bright spot in a world economy clouded by trade tensions.

The fiscal deficit sits at 7.2% of GDP, which is elevated and suggests the government is spending aggressively to support growth, a strategy that works only as long as interest rates remain manageable.
expert: India's 6.7% growth trajectory (tracking ahead of the 6.3% forecast) is being driven by tech export competitiveness and real wage expansion that has insulated domestic demand from global slowdown pressures, though the current account deficit of 1.2% GDP signals continued reliance on foreign capital inflows.

The policy rate of 6% remains restrictive relative to headline inflation expectations of 4.2%, suggesting the Reserve Bank of India retains room to ease if external pressures ease, a lever that could accelerate growth further into 2027.

The 7.2% fiscal deficit creates a medium-term vulnerability if capital flows reverse; India's ability to sustain high growth depends on continued inflows and export momentum in a deteriorating global trade environment where protectionism is rising.
